title: Ezekiel 37:1–14
context: Ezekiel 37:1–14 is the vision of the valley of dry bones, told by the prophet in the first person. The LORD’s hand brings Ezekiel by the Spirit into a valley full of very dry bones and asks, “Son of man, can these bones live?” Ezekiel answers, “Lord GOD, you know.” (37:3). At the LORD’s command he prophesies, and the bones come together and are covered with sinews, flesh, and skin, but there is no breath in them (37:4–8); then he prophesies to the wind, and breath enters them and they stand up, an exceedingly great army (37:9–10). The Hebrew word behind breath, wind, and Spirit in these verses is the same, and the vision plays on all three senses, from the breath that gives life (compare Genesis 2:7, “breathed into his nostrils the breath of life”) to the LORD’s promise, “I will put my Spirit in you, and you will live” (37:14; compare 36:26–27). The LORD himself interprets the vision: “these bones are the whole house of Israel”, a people who say, “Our bones are dried up, and our hope is lost.” (37:11). In context, the opened graves picture the nation brought back from exile and despair to life in its own land (37:12–14). Many readers in both traditions also see in the vision an image that anticipates bodily resurrection, comparing Daniel 12:2 and Isaiah 26:19 and later Christian hope such as John 5:28–29; others take the resurrection language as a vivid image of national restoration without a direct teaching about individual resurrection. Both readings appear in each tradition. The life-giving work of God’s Spirit in 37:14 is shared ground; how that renewing work relates to human response is discussed at the boxes at Deuteronomy 5:29 and Deuteronomy 10:16, with Ezekiel 11:19 and 36:26–27 as related promises in their own settings.

verses.text: The LORD’s hand was on me, and he brought me out in the LORD’s Spirit, and set me down in the middle of the valley; and it was full of bones.
verses.arminianNotes: Ezekiel says the LORD’s hand was on him and brought him out in the LORD’s Spirit into a valley full of bones. Arminian readers note that the vision begins with God’s initiative and the Spirit’s leading, and they see a prophet taken to the place of his people’s deepest despair.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the same initiative and observe that the scene of a valley of bones would have spoken powerfully to exiles who felt as good as dead. They read the opening as shared ground, since God brings his servant to see the condition he intends to reverse.

verses.text: He caused me to pass by them all around; and behold, there were very many in the open valley, and behold, they were very dry.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD caused Ezekiel to pass by the bones all around, and they were very many and very dry. Arminian readers note that the stress on dryness shows a situation beyond human remedy, and they see the vision preparing for a restoration that only God can accomplish.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the same emphasis and read the dryness as underlining the people’s helplessness. They observe that the vision is first about the nation’s condition in exile, and both traditions see in the scene a picture of hopelessness that God alone can answer.

verses.text: He said to me, “Son of man, can these bones live?” I answered, “Lord GOD, you know.”
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD asks, “Son of man, can these bones live?” Ezekiel answers, “Lord GOD, you know.” Arminian readers note the prophet’s humble answer, which leaves the outcome with God, and they see in it a fitting response of faith before a situation that seems impossible.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the same answer and read it as an acknowledgment that life depends entirely on God’s will and power. Both traditions see the exchange as shared ground, in which the question exposes human limits and the answer turns the prophet toward the LORD.

verses.text: Again he said to me, “Prophesy over these bones, and tell them, ‘You dry bones, hear the LORD’s word.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD tells Ezekiel to prophesy over the bones and say, “You dry bones, hear the LORD’s word.” Arminian readers note that God uses the prophet’s spoken word as the means of bringing life, and they see in this the importance of proclaiming God’s word even where response seems impossible.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the same use of the prophetic word and read it as God working through his appointed means. They observe that the command to address dry bones shows that the power lies in the LORD’s word, not in the hearers, a point both traditions affirm.

verses.text: The Lord GOD says to these bones: “Behold, I will cause breath to enter into you, and you will live.
verses.arminianNotes: The Lord GOD says to the bones, “Behold, I will cause breath to enter into you, and you will live.” Arminian readers note that the word for breath also means wind and spirit, and they see the promise of life as God’s gracious gift to a people who cannot give themselves life.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the same wordplay and the echo of Genesis 2:7, named without harmonizing. They read the promise as God’s sovereign giving of life, and both traditions treat it as shared ground that life comes from God’s breath.

verses.text: I will lay sinews on you, and will bring up flesh on you, and cover you with skin, and put breath in you, and you will live. Then you will know that I am the LORD.” ’ ”
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD promises to lay sinews, flesh, and skin on the bones and put breath in them, “Then you will know that I am the LORD.” Arminian readers note that the restoration aims at knowing God, and they see the promise as leading the people into a renewed relationship with him.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the recurring phrase you will know that I am the LORD, which runs through Ezekiel. They read the restoration as revealing God’s character and purposes, and both traditions see the knowledge of God as the goal of his saving acts.

verses.text: So I prophesied as I was commanded. As I prophesied, there was a noise, and behold, there was an earthquake. Then the bones came together, bone to its bone.
verses.arminianNotes: Ezekiel prophesied as commanded, and with a noise and an earthquake the bones came together, bone to its bone. Arminian readers note the prophet’s obedience and the immediate effect of God’s word, and they see the vision unfolding in stages that build anticipation.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the same obedience and read the earthquake and noise as signs of God’s powerful working. They observe that the restoration proceeds in order, and both traditions read the scene as shared ground on the effectiveness of God’s word spoken through his servant.

verses.text: I saw, and, behold, there were sinews on them, and flesh came up, and skin covered them above; but there was no breath in them.
verses.arminianNotes: Ezekiel saw sinews, flesh, and skin on the bones, “but there was no breath in them.” Arminian readers note that the bodies are complete yet lifeless, and they see a picture of outward restoration that still needs the gift of God’s life-giving breath to be complete.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the same two stages and read the lack of breath as showing that outward renewal is not enough without the Spirit. Both traditions treat the scene as shared ground, often comparing it with the need for inward renewal in 36:26–27.

verses.text: Then he said to me, “Prophesy to the wind, prophesy, son of man, and tell the wind, ‘The Lord GOD says: “Come from the four winds, breath, and breathe on these slain, that they may live.” ’ ”
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD tells Ezekiel, “Prophesy to the wind”, and to call breath from the four winds to breathe on the slain. Arminian readers note the wordplay on wind, breath, and spirit, all rendered from one Hebrew word, and they see the life of the nation coming from God’s Spirit.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the same wordplay and observe that the four winds suggest breath drawn from every direction. They read the verse as shared ground on the Spirit as the giver of life, while noting that the slain are called to life by God’s command, not by their own power.

verses.text: So I prophesied as he commanded me, and the breath came into them, and they lived, and stood up on their feet, an exceedingly great army.
verses.arminianNotes: Ezekiel prophesied, “and the breath came into them, and they lived, and stood up on their feet, an exceedingly great army.” Arminian readers note the dramatic completion of the vision, and they see the great army as a sign of the people’s restoration to strength and purpose.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the same climax and the echo of Genesis 2:7, where the breath of life makes man a living soul. They read the scene as God’s re-creation of his people, and both traditions treat it as shared ground on God’s power to give life.

verses.text: Then he said to me, “Son of man, these bones are the whole house of Israel. Behold, they say, ‘Our bones are dried up, and our hope is lost. We are completely cut off.’
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says, “Son of man, these bones are the whole house of Israel.” The people say their hope is lost. Arminian readers note that the LORD himself interprets the vision, and they see it first as an answer to the despair of exiles who felt cut off from life and hope.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the same interpretation and read the vision primarily as a promise of national restoration. They observe that the people’s words, “Our bones are dried up”, give the setting for the vision, and both traditions read the verse as shared ground.

verses.text: Therefore prophesy, and tell them, ‘The Lord GOD says: “Behold, I will open your graves, and cause you to come up out of your graves, my people; and I will bring you into the land of Israel.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says, “Behold, I will open your graves, and cause you to come up out of your graves, my people; and I will bring you into the land of Israel.” Arminian readers note that the graves picture exile, and they see the promise of return as God’s faithfulness to his people.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the same reading of graves as exile and observe that many in both traditions also see an anticipation of bodily resurrection (compare Daniel 12:2; Isaiah 26:19). They hold that reading as a hedged extension rather than the verse’s primary sense.

verses.text: You will know that I am the LORD, when I have opened your graves and caused you to come up out of your graves, my people.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says, “You will know that I am the LORD, when I have opened your graves and caused you to come up out of your graves, my people.” Arminian readers note the tender phrase my people, and they see God’s restoration as a renewal of the covenant relationship.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the same phrase and read the opening of graves as revealing God’s power and faithfulness. They observe that Christian readers have often heard in such language an anticipation of resurrection hope, such as John 5:28–29, while holding the national sense as primary.

verses.text: I will put my Spirit in you, and you will live. Then I will place you in your own land; and you will know that I, the LORD, have spoken it and performed it,” says the LORD.’ ”
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says, “I will put my Spirit in you, and you will live.” Arminian readers see the Spirit’s life-giving work as God’s gracious renewal that enables a real response, and they see the box at Deuteronomy 5:29 for how their tradition relates grace and human response.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the Spirit’s work as God’s effectual giving of life that produces the response it calls for, and they see the box at Deuteronomy 10:16, with Ezekiel 11:19 and 36:26–27 as related promises. Both traditions confess the gift of the Spirit as the heart of the restoration.
